narrative.text: The back cover text of the Arabic edition of the WHO–ITU National eHealth Strategy Toolkit, describing the growing role of ICT in supporting health services; the opening characters are garbled.
A near-blank title page of the Arabic National eHealth Strategy Toolkit, with garbled logo text.
The cataloguing and copyright page of the Arabic National eHealth Strategy Toolkit, with subject headings, ISBNs and disclaimers.

The foreword of the Arabic eHealth strategy toolkit, in which WHO and ITU present it as a product of their long collaboration and of their governing bodies' interest in national eHealth strategies. It invites countries to use it in pursuing ambitious national eHealth projects.
The acknowledgements of the Arabic eHealth strategy toolkit, naming the WHO and ITU steering committee and contributors, and thanking those who prepared the Arabic translation.
A short table of contents listing the toolkit's introduction and its three parts: national eHealth vision, action plan, and monitoring and evaluation.

Introduces the National eHealth Strategy Toolkit, explaining its purpose and intended users. It notes how eHealth makes health systems more efficient and responsive, and that the toolkit provides a framework and method for developing a national eHealth vision, action plan and monitoring framework in three successive parts.

Describes the three parts of the toolkit, with Part 1 developing a national eHealth vision that explains why a national approach is needed, what it should achieve and how. It sets out the why, what and how elements and says the toolkit gives governments a solid basis for developing and implementing their vision.
A repeat of the back cover text of the Arabic eHealth strategy toolkit on the growing role of ICT in health care, with the same garbled opening characters.
The title page of Part 1 of the Arabic eHealth toolkit, on developing a national eHealth vision, with garbled logo text.
A divider page for Part 1 of the Arabic eHealth toolkit, on developing a national eHealth vision, with some garbled characters.
The cataloguing and copyright page for Part 1 of the Arabic eHealth toolkit, with subject headings and disclaimers.

Introduces Part 1 of the toolkit as a resource for countries developing or revitalizing an eHealth strategy, and outlines its chapters. These cover the national context, the vision framework, the method, managing the process and stakeholder engagement, with later chapters on gathering and analysing information.
The table of contents of Part 1 of the eHealth toolkit, listing chapters on national context, the vision framework, the method, process management and stakeholder engagement, plus annexes.
A list of figures in Part 1 of the eHealth toolkit, including national context, eHealth components, the vision framework and governance models.
A list of tables in Part 1 of the eHealth toolkit, covering eHealth impacts, national context, strategy focus, component roles and prioritization factors.

Opens Chapter 1 on the national eHealth context, explaining that health work increasingly depends on information and communications, and giving WHO's definition of eHealth as the use of ICT for health. It describes eHealth benefits for health goals and wider development, citing WHO's eHealth observatory and governing body resolutions.

Describes how WHO and ITU governing bodies encouraged countries to develop national eHealth strategies, stressing the roles of health and ICT ministries in coordinated action, policy consensus and private sector engagement. The page ends with garbled, partly reversed Latin-script reference text.

Table 1 lists examples of eHealth's impact, such as personalized care across the life course, care at home and work, and remote consultation and learning. The text then explains that eHealth development depends on both the ICT environment and an enabling environment of governance, policy, legislation, standards and workforce; the page ends with garbled reference text.

Presents a figure of the national context for eHealth based on the maturity of the ICT and enabling environments, and describes three stages: early adoption, development and scale-up. It begins describing a country in the early stage, where projects are fragmented and largely donor funded.

Describes the early-adoption context in which eHealth relies on donors and consultants and a country may not meet international reporting obligations, driven by access and quality of care, with examples like telemedicine. It then describes the development stage, where vertical health information systems grow at high cost.

Explains that in the development stage the national plan should strengthen the enabling environment, legal trust and standards to avoid ever-larger vertical systems. It then describes the scale-up stage, where focus shifts to efficient services, data use for planning, privacy policies and monitoring.

Table 2 summarizes the three national contexts for eHealth, from small, unsustainable pilot projects to broader adoption and integration. The text then contrasts comprehensive and focused planning approaches and says a national strategy adds value at every stage.

Table 3 sets out the strategic context and focus for an eHealth strategy at each stage, from building awareness and foundations to scaling up services and setting privacy and security policies. It then introduces the building-block components of a national eHealth environment.

Table 4 describes the roles of the seven eHealth components, divided between the enabling environment and the ICT environment. They are leadership and governance, strategy and investment, legislation and policy, workforce, standards and interoperability, infrastructure, and services and applications.

Opens Chapter 2 on the framework for a national eHealth vision, which explains why a national approach is needed, what it will achieve and how. A figure links strategic context, vision, outcomes and required components, with the strategic context covering population health, health system status, national health strategy and development priorities.

Explains how health goals and challenges point to areas where ICT investment adds value, and how the strategic context leads to an eHealth vision describing the eHealth-enabled health system. It notes that recommendations form the starting point for the action plan in Part 2 and refers to a proposed vision document structure in an annex.

Opens Chapter 3 with an overview of the method for developing a national eHealth vision, based on lessons from countries with existing strategies. It describes drafting an initial unconstrained vision, refining it against the current environment and producing recommendations, with stakeholder engagement throughout.

Outlines (in Arabic) the method for building a national eHealth vision in the National eHealth Strategy Toolkit, starting with developing the strategic context from population health, the health system and wider development goals. It goes on to describe drafting an initial vision, identifying the eHealth components required and reviewing the current eHealth environment to balance ambition with realism.

Describes the final stages of developing the national eHealth vision: assessing opportunities to reuse components and gaps to address, then refining the vision and making strategic recommendations that feed into Part 2 of the toolkit.

Opens the chapter on managing the process of developing a national eHealth vision, explaining why effective leadership and governance matter. It lists what is needed, such as high-level sector leadership, governance structures, a skilled multidisciplinary team and an agreed timeline and resources.

Explains the need for sustained leadership and a respected champion to drive the eHealth vision and introduces a governance structure for the work. A figure shows an example governance model linking health sector leadership, the project team and stakeholder reference groups.

Tabulates examples of governance bodies for developing the eHealth vision with their tasks, responsibilities and membership. It then explains the value of a project-based approach and a core team with health system and public health expertise, drawing on other government bodies and the private sector as needed.

Lists the skills and experience the core project team should have, such as knowledge of national health needs, strategic planning, stakeholder engagement and information technology. It stresses early planning of internal coordination and documentation and introduces example timelines of 12 to 19 weeks.
A figure showing two sample timelines for developing a national eHealth vision, with expected minimum and maximum durations for each activity.

Opens the chapter on stakeholder engagement, explaining that a well-supported eHealth vision requires working with multidisciplinary stakeholders in line with the government's role. It lists the steps of identifying stakeholder groups, planning how to manage them and defining consultation points.

Explains how the government's role shapes the strategy development process and the type of stakeholder involvement. It begins listing health sector stakeholders, such as professional associations, hospitals, academics, insurers, patient groups and the public.

Continues listing stakeholders, including public health authorities, private providers, ICT vendors and media, as well as those outside the health sector. It advises the team to prioritize those most affected by or able to influence the strategy.

Describes four common stakeholder roles in developing a national eHealth vision, distinguished by contribution, influence and interest. A figure and table give examples of stakeholders in each role, from senior decision-makers to community groups and individuals.

Explains choosing an engagement approach for each stakeholder group, linked to a communication plan, and notes that face-to-face consultation with the general public is usually limited. It introduces the need for a consultation plan setting out how, when and why each stakeholder group will be consulted.
A sample stakeholder consultation plan showing for each group at which stages it is consulted, reviews or approves outputs, from the strategic context through to the final vision.

Advises minimizing repeated consultations with the same stakeholders by spreading them over several rounds. A table gives a sample consultation approach, with questions and formats such as interviews, small group forums and teleconferences.

Opens the chapter on developing the strategic context, whose aim is to describe the health system goals and challenges that eHealth can help address. It lists the research activities involved and the expected outputs on strategic priorities and the potential role of eHealth.

Describes researching population health and demographics, with a table of questions on population size, age, socioeconomic groups and disease burden over the next 10–20 years. It recommends desk research supplemented by interviews with ministries and agencies responsible for health monitoring and planning.

Describes the step of understanding the national health system, including the cost, quality and accessibility of services and how it is managed. A table lists dimensions to explore, such as service types, unmet needs, providers, workforce and financing, and the expected outputs.

Explains how to gather information on the health system from national and local agencies and international reports, supported by stakeholder interviews. It also covers identifying the national health strategy, its goals, planned reforms and future financing.

Describes agreeing on strategic health themes, goals and priorities with health sector leaders, noting that some countries lack a clear health strategy. It also covers identifying non-health drivers relevant to eHealth, such as wider social and economic development goals.

Describes internal analysis of regional and international commitments, such as the Millennium Development Goals, to understand their implications for eHealth. It then explains selecting the goals and challenges on which eHealth can have the greatest impact as the basis for the vision.
A table of common strategic goals and challenges across population health, health services, workforce and wider development, with guidance on validating them with key stakeholders to build consensus.

Explains describing how eHealth will support the selected goals by examining health information flows and the changes needed in them. It lists expected outputs, including how sharing and accessing health information can address health and non-health goals.

Opens the chapter on learning from eHealth trends and experience in other countries, including successes and failures. The expected outputs are an understanding of how eHealth is used in similar settings, the goals it can address and evidence of its benefits.

Describes researching other countries' national eHealth visions, strategies and programmes to draw lessons, such as their goals, governance and results. It advises checking early whether countries have dedicated eHealth bodies and using WHO and other international reports.

Recommends exploratory interviews, study tours or regional meetings with people responsible for eHealth in other countries to supplement desk research. It also describes researching international eHealth trends and best practice using government, industry and academic sources.

Opens the chapter on drafting an initial, unconstrained national eHealth vision describing how eHealth will help achieve health goals. Its outputs include a vision statement, eHealth outcomes, stakeholder implications and optional scenarios.

Describes agreeing the time horizon for the eHealth vision, considering the national health strategy and planning cycles. It then introduces defining the eHealth outcomes that form the basis for identifying required components.

Presents a table of sample questions for defining eHealth outcomes, covering areas such as health system planning, models of care, access, workforce, quality and safety of care. It advises discussing these outcomes with stakeholders until the vision statement is drafted.

Describes linking eHealth outcomes to the strategic context so the vision clearly shows how it addresses health system goals and stakeholder needs. Without this rationale, it warns, the vision may lack credibility, and the rationale should be refined after the vision statement is drafted.

Describes preparing a high-level, non-technology-driven initial vision statement that decision-makers can endorse and communicate easily. It lists what the statement should convey, such as the expected benefits for the health system and the eHealth outcomes sought.

Explains drafting the vision statement through internal working sessions and review with a small group of stakeholders, deferring wider consultation. It then introduces describing the implications of the vision for each stakeholder group, including current problems and expected improvements.

A sample national eHealth vision for health care providers in 2020, describing better decisions at the point of care through access to complete information and decision support. It then introduces developing scenarios that show the challenges eHealth will address.

Presents a sample scenario of a woman and her family in a rural area of East Africa, showing how eHealth would change her experience of diagnosis, treatment and follow-up for a chronic condition. It describes how electronic records, telehealth and mobile services would help her care across health facilities. The scenario ends by noting that her quality of life and life expectancy would improve and she could keep working and caring for her family.
Explains that scenario development is a creative exercise that can draw on example eHealth services and should be reviewed and refined with stakeholders.
Opens the chapter on identifying the eHealth components required to deliver the initial vision, including their relationships and dependencies.

Describes identifying the leadership and governance components needed to direct and coordinate national, regional and local eHealth activities. A table gives examples of governance functions, and outputs include roles, responsibilities and relationships between governance bodies.

Advises defining the leadership and governance model through internal working sessions. It then describes identifying the strategy and investment components needed to develop, operate and sustain the national eHealth environment.

Describes identifying the eHealth services and applications needed to meet health system goals and enable people, providers and managers to access and share information. A table lists example service categories, from care delivery to health programme management, policy development and research.

Covers the expected outputs and method for identifying services and applications, linking them back to eHealth outcomes. It then introduces identifying the infrastructure components that support information exchange across the health sector.

Describes the physical computing, network and software infrastructure components required to host eHealth applications and exchange information. It advises explaining why each component is needed by linking it to eHealth outcomes.

An example linking an infrastructure component, high-speed data links for rural telehealth, to an eHealth outcome of reducing workforce shortages. The page then begins describing standards components, such as terminology and medicines standards.
Describes the eHealth standards components, such as message structures, transfer protocols and data standards for clinical terminology, diagnosis and treatment, including for HIV/AIDS.
Notes that other enabling components may emerge and introduces identifying the legislation, policy and compliance components needed to support the national eHealth environment.

Advises identifying legislation, policy and compliance components through internal working sessions and linking them back to eHealth outcomes, directly or through services, infrastructure and standards components.
Describes preparing non-technical architecture models of the required eHealth components to communicate them to senior stakeholders, with a component map as one example.

A figure showing a sample component map of a national eHealth environment, covering individual electronic health records, health service delivery functions and supporting components; some extracted text at the end is garbled.

Presents Figure 10, a stakeholder perspective model showing what eHealth could mean for health consumers, such as access to health information, online portals and remote monitoring. It also explains how to build a national eHealth component map; a footnote at the bottom is garbled, reversed Latin-script text.
Opens chapter 10 on gathering information about the current eHealth environment, organised across seven component areas from leadership and governance to workforce.

Gives sample questions for gathering information on eHealth leadership and governance and on strategy and investment, such as existing coordination bodies and national health priorities. A footnote in Latin script is garbled in the extraction.

Continues the sample questions with funding mechanisms and past strategies that did not succeed, then turns to existing eHealth services and applications. The page ends with a garbled Latin-script footnote.

Lists questions about eHealth infrastructure, including unique identifiers, adoption of information and communication technology and electronic health record repositories. It then sets out questions on standards and interoperability already in use in the country.

Asks about past standards initiatives that failed and about legislation, data protection and privacy rules affecting eHealth. It also covers policies on innovation, and carries a garbled Latin-script footnote.

Covers questions on compliance policy and on the eHealth workforce, including skills, accreditation and education programmes. It then describes internal desk research, drawing on sources such as WHO and ITU reports.

Lists the stakeholder groups to consult when gathering information, such as care providers, industry, health managers and chief information officers. It stresses that this step is about collecting information rather than judging it.
Introduces chapter 11 on assessing opportunities, gaps, risks and barriers in the national eHealth environment. It sets out the purpose of the step and the outputs it should produce.

Explains how to compare existing eHealth components with those the vision requires, looking at reuse, sharing, gaps and risks. Sample questions cover whether components need modification and over what timeframe.
Gives further assessment questions on cost, stakeholder involvement and identifying gaps. It then lists risk questions on political support, funding and building consensus.

Describes the recommended outputs of the assessment and sets out a four-step internal assessment process. It closes with guidance on consulting stakeholders, followed by a garbled Latin-script footnote.
Introduces chapter 12 on refining the eHealth vision and drafting strategic recommendations. Expected outputs include an ambitious but realistic vision, its endorsement and its dissemination.
Advises setting the scope and focus of the vision, noting that countries begin from different starting points. It states that preparing a business case falls outside this part of the toolkit.
Shows Figure 12 and Table 25 on the steps for refining the vision. It explains that prioritisation at this stage is strategic, with programme-level priorities left to Part 2.
Poses questions to guide refinement of the initial eHealth vision. It describes this as an internal activity whose results are then reviewed by stakeholders.
Explains how to develop high-level, outcome-focused strategic recommendations for each eHealth component area. A worked example concerns establishing a unique health identifier service.

Gives a second example recommendation about incentives for care providers to invest in eHealth where computing infrastructure is weak. It then covers disseminating the vision through a period of education and awareness-raising.
Notes that the consultation period on the vision varies in length, overlaps with mobilising the Part 2 team, and is followed by a review for funding.

Begins Annex A with examples of eHealth services drawn from the Global Observatory for eHealth. These include electronic medical records, telehealth, remote patient monitoring and interactive services.
Continues the annex examples with telecare for elderly and disabled people. It also describes practice management and patient management systems.
Describes examples of electronic prescribing and medication services and of health information systems. A garbled Latin-script footnote appears on the page.
Presents Table 26 with examples of eHealth benefits, such as better access to care in rural areas and access to second opinions. The footnotes in Latin script are garbled.
Sets out Annex C, a suggested structure for a national eHealth vision document. It lists the sections such a document might contain.
Presents Table 27 in Annex D, summarising the overall method for developing a national eHealth vision. It condenses the chapters and their main steps into one table.
A near-empty page carrying only the running header and footer of Annex D.
Shows the first part of Figure 13, an example national eHealth component map. It sets out components such as leadership and governance, strategy and infrastructure.
Continues the example component map with services, standards, legislation and workforce components.
Describes Annex F on the governance continuum, contrasting bureaucratic, market and network forms of governance. A garbled Latin-script footnote appears at the end.
Provides Annex G, definitions of terms used in the toolkit. These include strategic goals, outputs, activities and output and outcome indicators.
The back cover of Part 1, describing the toolkit as a WHO–ITU collaboration on understanding and applying eHealth, followed by garbled barcode and Latin-script text.
A section divider page for Part 2 of the toolkit, on developing a national eHealth action plan.
The title page of Part 2 of the toolkit, on developing a national eHealth action plan.
The cataloguing and copyright page for the toolkit, with subject headings, ISBN and WHO disclaimer and printing notes.

Introduces Part 2, explaining that it builds on the national eHealth vision and outputs from Part 1 to produce an action plan. It notes the plan needs a skilled team and that Part 3 focuses on monitoring and refining the plan.

Gives an overview of the three-part toolkit and of how Part 2 is organised. It outlines the purpose of each chapter, from summarising Part 1 outputs to detailed guidance on each planning stage, and lists the annexes.
The table of contents for Part 2, listing its nine chapters and seven annexes with page numbers.
A list of the figures and boxes in Part 2, with page numbers.
A list of the tables in Part 2, with page numbers, covering governance mechanisms, stakeholder roles and examples of eHealth risks.
A blank page with no text.

Introduces the move from vision to action plan, noting that the government has by now produced and endorsed a national eHealth vision. It explains that the action plan lets government identify, fund and coordinate the components and work closely with multisectoral stakeholders.

Presents Figure 2, a framework for an eHealth action plan built around action lines, activities, resources and strategic phases. It stresses that the quality, cost and availability of human, supplier and infrastructure resources shape the plan's scope and timing.

Explains that action plans are usually complex and that dividing them into strategic phases eases planning and funding, with early phases planned in more detail. It also points to a suggested plan structure in Annex A.

Opens chapter 2 with Figure 3, the method for developing an eHealth action plan, and describes managing the process and engaging stakeholders. It then explains that planning starts by identifying the activities needed and grouping them into action lines.

Describes combining the action line plans into one integrated action plan checked against the Part 1 priorities. It argues that a phased approach is both strategic and practical, helping stakeholders understand what each phase should achieve.

Introduces chapter 3 on managing the process of developing the action plan. It lists the main tasks, such as adapting governance from Part 1, securing skills and setting a timetable, and the expected output.

Stresses that senior ministerial and health sector leadership remains as important for the action plan as it was for the vision. It then shows Figure 4, a model governance structure adapted from Part 1.

Presents Table 1 on proposed governance mechanisms for preparing the action plan, from health sector leadership to the wider stakeholder environment. It then lists the skills and experience the core Part 2 team should have, such as national strategic project management.
Completes the list of skills needed by the core team and gives Figure 5, a sample timeline of 9 to 15 weeks for developing the action plan.

Introduces chapter 4 on engaging stakeholders, which aims to secure broad support for a realistic action plan. Tasks include clarifying government's role, identifying stakeholder groups and planning when to consult them.

Discusses the role of government in developing the action plan, which can range from directive to collaborative. It lists typical health-sector stakeholders, such as professional associations, academic institutions, insurers, patient groups and private providers.

Notes that stakeholders outside the health sector, such as other ministries, may contribute resources or have strong interests in eHealth. It sets out stakeholder categories including decision-makers, key influencers and subject experts.

Presents Table 3 describing common stakeholder roles, from those who set the vision and approve the plan to experts and wider stakeholders affected by funding priorities. Examples are given for each role, such as professional associations and patient advocacy groups.

Advises tailoring the engagement approach to each stakeholder group's role and interests, as in Table 4. It recommends a structured engagement plan that saves time and limits repeated consultation of the same stakeholders.

Presents Table 5, a sample stakeholder consultation plan showing which groups are consulted at each stage and for what input. It covers topics such as securing skills and resources and the funding needed for eHealth programmes.

Introduces chapter 5 on developing individual plans for each eHealth action line. It lists the steps, including identifying interdependencies and risks, and the expected output of an indicative plan per action line.
Describes the step of defining the main eHealth action lines, which group activities with a shared focus or purpose. It recommends ending with four to six main action lines, each with a clear focus.

Warns against listing too many activities, since the plan should stay high-level. It explains that activities are drawn from each Part 1 strategic recommendation and that draft action lines can be tested with a few stakeholders.

Describes in Arabic, from Part 2 of the WHO-ITU National eHealth Strategy Toolkit on developing a national eHealth action plan, the step of breaking the strategic recommendations from Part 1 into outputs and assigning them to action lines for governance, foundations, solutions, and change and adoption. A box gives examples of outputs for a recommendation to implement a national unique health identifier service.

Explains in Arabic that mapping outputs to action lines should be done in internal workshops, revisiting or adding action lines where outputs do not fit, and that identifying who may lead each output helps define the stakeholders responsible for delivering the eHealth action lines.

Sets out in Arabic the expected output of describing high-level activities for each eHealth action line, including scope, duration and dependencies, with a table of example activities for governance, foundations, solutions, and change and adoption, such as creating a national eHealth governance board.

Describes in Arabic how activities for each action line should be identified through internal workshops based on the strategic recommendations, and stresses multisectoral consultation with health and non-health stakeholders who may be responsible for carrying them out.

Notes in Arabic that change and adoption activities should be defined alongside other action line activities, then introduces the step of identifying dependencies between activities across action lines, which can arise from timing and other factors and affect sequencing.

Presents in Arabic an example action line plan for the foundations line, showing activities with high-level timing and sequencing, and explains that each plan can be accompanied by a list of stakeholders with leadership roles; the figure labels are partly garbled.

Describes in Arabic the step of identifying risks to delivering the action line plans, across areas such as leadership and governance, stakeholder engagement, resources and funding, ways of working and external dependencies, as input to integrating the overall action plan.

Explains in Arabic the optional step of refining the initial set of eHealth action lines, for example when many activities do not fit, a line has too few outputs, or a line is too complex to communicate.

Introduces in Arabic the phase of developing an integrated eHealth action plan by combining the individual action line plans and checking alignment with health system priorities, stakeholders and funders, listing its main activities.

Describes in Arabic the step of drafting the integrated action plan, which requires accounting for dependencies between activities in different action lines and for mitigating identified risks, which may change the sequence of activities.

Explains in Arabic that drafting the action plan involves internal workshops with limited stakeholder consultation, in two steps: combining and resequencing the action line plans by dependencies, then refining the combined plan to reduce risks, some of which will remain.

Describes in Arabic how to check the action plan's alignment with health system priorities and stakeholder and funder expectations through internal analysis and consultation, with a table of steps and example questions to guide the review.

Describes in Arabic the step of identifying programme-level risks to implementing the eHealth action plan, offering example questions about scope, timeframe, capacity for change, resources, dependencies and whether stakeholders consider the plan achievable.
Explains in Arabic how the action plan is refined to improve alignment with strategic priorities, for example by resequencing activities, adjusting their scope or reconsidering certain activities.

Introduces in Arabic the phase of identifying, at a high level, the resources needed to deliver the eHealth action plan, starting with understanding the skills and expertise required and the country's constraints in obtaining them.

Describes in Arabic the step of identifying the skills and expertise needed to deliver the action plan, with a table of dimensions such as clinical practice change, programme management and technical skills.

Notes in Arabic the value of input from subject experts on the skills and resources needed, then describes identifying national constraints on obtaining the required skills and expertise, which differ by country.

Describes in Arabic the step of choosing how to secure the needed skills and expertise, with a table of approaches such as direct hiring, contracting firms and technology suppliers, and partnerships with other organisations.
A table in Arabic of dimensions for choosing how to secure skills and expertise, including identified constraints, timing, duration, government workforce policies and availability.

Describes in Arabic the step of estimating the funding needed to deliver the eHealth action plan, influenced by the scope of resources, how skills are secured, ICT capital and operating costs, and change and adoption mechanisms such as incentive programmes.

Presents in Arabic a suggested approach to estimating funding needs, combining top-down estimates based on comparable programmes with bottom-up estimates built from activities, including ICT and non-ICT costs; the figure text is partly garbled.

Continues in Arabic the funding estimation approach, covering ICT infrastructure capital and operating estimates for each activity and additional funding such as incentives, and notes that top-down and bottom-up estimates can be used together.
Introduces in Arabic the phase of applying funding constraints, which assesses the size and timing of available financial resources so the action plan can be revised to be realistic and achievable.

Describes in Arabic the step of assessing likely funding availability across the wider funding environment, with a table of potential sources such as government departments, regional bodies, donors and other organisations.

Advises in Arabic learning how other countries financed national eHealth programmes and holding dialogue with health sector and other government decision-makers to clarify how much funding is likely to be available.

Describes in Arabic how to agree on refining the action plan in light of available funds, through internal analysis and consultation with decision-makers, with a table of steps for developing, assessing and selecting options.

Describes in Arabic the step of revising the action plan according to the preferred funding option, producing a plan achievable within likely funding by resequencing, rescoping or reconsidering activities.

Introduces in Arabic the phase of defining implementation phases, which present the often complex eHealth action plan in an easily understood way and set eHealth development and use objectives for each phase.

Describes in Arabic the step of identifying logical implementation phases in the action plan, each showing the strategic focus for a period, with a figure mapping action lines across three phases and monitoring and evaluation timeframes.

Describes in Arabic the step of defining communication messages for each implementation phase, telling decision-makers and stakeholders the strategic focus, tangible outputs and progress toward the national eHealth vision.

Explains in Arabic the step of setting objectives for each implementation phase in terms of improvements for key stakeholder groups, with a box of example objectives for a first connection phase, such as starting to identify consumers uniquely through health identifiers. The page header text is garbled.
Notes in Arabic that setting phase objectives is an internal activity analysing what each activity will deliver and how it will improve stakeholders' interaction with the health system.

Annex A in Arabic, proposing a structure and table of contents for a national eHealth action plan document and advising that it be made accessible to a wide audience, with sections ordered to suit readers.

Annex B in Arabic, a table summarising the methodology for developing a national eHealth action plan, phase by phase, from managing the process and stakeholder engagement to action lines, resources, funding constraints and implementation phases.
Annex C in Arabic, introducing a figure that maps the eHealth action lines onto the eHealth component map from Part 1 of the toolkit.
The continuation of the Arabic figure mapping eHealth components to action lines, with only its caption and page reference extracted.

Annex D in Arabic, giving further examples of possible activities in the four common eHealth action lines, beginning with governance activities that establish structures for accountability, transparency and leadership of a national eHealth programme.

Describes in Arabic foundations activities, which provide the components needed for secure exchange of health information and electronic access to services and are best delivered through a nationally coordinated approach, with a table of examples such as designing foundation services and assessing existing agencies.

Lists in Arabic further foundations activities on computing infrastructure and data connectivity for health care providers, and introduces solutions activities aimed at overcoming poor computing infrastructure that can hinder eHealth adoption.

A table in Arabic of example solutions activities, such as creating a national eHealth solutions investment fund, setting up a solution compliance function and designing and deploying priority national eHealth services, followed by the start of change and adoption activities.

A table in Arabic of example change and adoption activities, such as identifying priority consumers, providers and organisations, assessing their readiness, running eHealth awareness campaigns and creating a framework to measure the effectiveness of adoption efforts.

Annex E in Arabic, giving examples of risks associated with eHealth activities, beginning with leadership and governance risks such as the lack of a credible senior leader and inadequate governance and oversight mechanisms.

Lists in Arabic examples of resource and funding risks for eHealth activities, such as scarce skills, competition for resources from other programmes, insufficient capacity, uneven geographic distribution of resources and lack of funding.
An Arabic annex on public-private partnerships, defining them, listing reasons governments use them such as value for money and risk sharing, and introducing common types of arrangements.
Describes in Arabic further public-private partnership models, such as build-lease-transfer and build-operate-share-transfer, and notes that such partnerships are complex and need thorough review.
An Arabic glossary of terms used in the eHealth toolkit, defining strategic goals and challenges, eHealth outcomes and the eHealth vision; the page header text is garbled.

The Arabic back cover of the National eHealth Strategy Toolkit, describing it as a practical expert guide from WHO and ITU for developing a national eHealth vision, action plan and monitoring framework, adaptable to any country, with partly garbled ISBN text.
A near-blank Arabic divider page for the monitoring and evaluation part, with garbled characters and a part number that appears misread.
A near-blank Arabic divider page for Part 3 on monitoring and evaluation.

The Arabic cataloguing and copyright page for Part 3 (monitoring and evaluation) of the WHO-ITU eHealth toolkit, 2013, with subject headings, ISBNs and WHO publication ordering and permissions details, partly garbled.

The Arabic-language opening of Part 3 of the National eHealth Strategy Toolkit, on monitoring and evaluation, stating its purpose of building a framework to monitor the action plan from Part 2 and evaluate outcomes. It names senior government and health sector staff as the target audience and recaps the three parts of the toolkit.
An Arabic-language orientation page outlining how Part 3 is organised, from the introduction through chapters on the framework and detailed guidance, plus annexes with definitions.

The Arabic-language table of contents for Part 3, listing chapters on the monitoring and evaluation framework, indicators, baselines and targets, governance and conclusions, and annexes on results-based management and example strategies.
An Arabic-language list of the figures and tables in Part 3, covering items such as the results chain, framework components, indicator relationships, governance models and example eHealth strategies.

Introduces in Arabic the assessment of progress and results, noting that by this stage a national eHealth vision and action plan should exist with lines of action, outputs, dependencies and resources. It introduces the monitoring and evaluation framework; the end of the extracted page contains garbled OCR in mixed scripts.

Distinguishes in Arabic the national eHealth monitoring and evaluation framework from programme management, which tracks inputs, activities and outputs of the action plan. The page ends with garbled OCR of what appear to be source citations.

States in Arabic that a national monitoring and evaluation framework needs dedicated resources and should be costed as part of eHealth planning, and refers to the results chain and results-based management annex.

Describes in Arabic the components of an eHealth monitoring and evaluation framework: indicators, baseline and target measures, and governance and processes. It explains that both output indicators on eHealth adoption and outcome indicators on results are needed.
Explains in Arabic that monitoring needs baseline and target measures over time, and that national governance should oversee monitoring and step in when results diverge from aims.

Gives an Arabic-language overview of the sequential method for developing the framework, from defining indicators to setting baselines and targets and then governance. It advises linking indicators to existing health reporting timeframes to avoid separate reporting.

Summarises in Arabic the steps of setting baseline and target measures for each indicator and defining governance and processes, noting that monitoring happens at several levels and by several parties.

Opens Chapter 3 in Arabic on defining eHealth indicators, which should be linked to stakeholders and outcomes from Part 1 so that real success is measured, not just implementation. It names the expected outputs as output indicators and outcome indicators.

Describes in Arabic the step of prioritising health and non-health stakeholders for whom showing eHealth results matters most, describing them as organisations or roles rather than individuals. It then explains exploring what each outcome would mean to each stakeholder.

An Arabic-language figure and guidance linking stakeholders, eHealth outcomes and indicators, with examples of expected improvements such as better rural access to primary care and support for pregnant women in remote areas. Other examples cover vaccine and medicine supply and researchers' access to evidence.

Explains in Arabic how this step draws on the eHealth outcomes set in the national vision, refining them into concrete results for each stakeholder. It then introduces identifying the outputs linked to each outcome; the page ends with garbled OCR.

An Arabic-language table of example eHealth outputs mapped to outcomes such as rural access to care, support for pregnant women and information sharing between care providers. The step builds on outputs developed in Part 2 of the toolkit.

Describes in Arabic reviewing and confirming focus areas with priority stakeholders, which shows the relative importance of outcomes and outputs given limited monitoring resources. It also notes the chance to build stakeholder support and gather their input.

An Arabic-language figure on the link between eHealth outcomes and output indicators, explaining that output indicators track gradual delivery such as data network roll-out or software adoption. It states that the step should yield useful indicators, shown in a table.

An Arabic-language table of example outcome indicators, such as percentage reductions in the time to detect and contain outbreaks and in the cost of reporting them. It also includes perception-based indicators on challenges to eHealth use.

An Arabic-language table pairing eHealth outcome indicators with output indicators, such as the share of care providers with fit-for-purpose connectivity and computing infrastructure. It covers areas including outbreak detection and reporting.

An Arabic-language table of suggested criteria for choosing indicators, such as being linked to outcomes and outputs, concrete and measurable, based on available data, and valid and verifiable. It helps screen candidate indicators.
Opens Chapter 4 in Arabic on setting baseline and target measures for each indicator. It outlines the purpose and the steps involved.

Describes in Arabic setting national monitoring and evaluation timeframes, which let government check whether the plan delivers results, spot problems needing correction and report regularly to stakeholders. It sets out the expected outputs of this step.

Explains in Arabic that monitoring timeframes should match the timing of eHealth activity, then describes setting a baseline for each output and outcome indicator. It notes that assessing progress depends on knowing the starting point.

Describes in Arabic setting target measures for output indicators before outcome indicators, since outcomes depend on outputs, and stresses realistic, achievable targets. It introduces the method for setting these targets.

Lists in Arabic inputs for setting output targets, such as external research on other national programmes and relationships between indicators. It also notes that action plan targets set earlier should be used as inputs.

Explains in Arabic that targets for outcome indicators are set much like output targets, through internal analysis of related output targets and baselines. It lists guiding questions for this analysis.
Opens Chapter 5 in Arabic on defining governance and processes for national monitoring and evaluation, aimed at bringing all actors together.

Describes in Arabic defining a governance model for national monitoring and evaluation of eHealth adoption and outcomes, setting out its functions and structure. It distinguishes this model from wider programme management governance.

An Arabic-language table of governance roles for monitoring and evaluation and the responsible parties, such as the ministry of health, subject experts, NGOs and international agencies like WHO and ITU. Roles include expert analytical support and wider research capacity.

Explains in Arabic that individual eHealth programmes, including external projects, monitor their own progress within the national framework so project performance feeds national indicators. A table sets out governance mechanisms and their roles in national monitoring.

Describes in Arabic sector and non-health-sector monitoring teams that track eHealth outputs and outcomes in parts of the health sector and in related sectors such as ICT. It notes their focus on wider social and economic development.

Describes in Arabic defining an ongoing national monitoring and evaluation process based on the work programme and indicator timeframes. It notes that detailed activity-level processes are not the focus of this step.

An Arabic-language list of national and activity-level monitoring and evaluation tasks, such as setting schedules, preparing tools and templates, advising teams on indicators, collecting reports and explaining variances. It also covers preparing reports for decision-makers.

The Arabic-language conclusion of the toolkit, stating that it guides countries in developing an eHealth vision, action plan and monitoring framework. It stresses that the outputs reflect a point in time and should be revisited.

Introduces in Arabic the annex on results-based management, noting that organisations seek to show they deliver as expected. It defines the aim as shifting management from processes to performance and results.
Explains in Arabic that results-based management combines top-down planning from goals to inputs with bottom-up management from inputs to results. It describes how this applies to programmes.

An Arabic-language figure linking monitoring and evaluation to the results chain, explaining that monitoring measures implementation while evaluation measures change and impact. It lists requirements for an effective monitoring and evaluation programme.

Introduces in Arabic a table of example national and state eHealth strategies from several countries, noting they predate the toolkit and do not follow its approach. The page includes some garbled OCR.

An Arabic-language glossary-style annex defining toolkit terms such as strategic goals and challenges, eHealth outcomes, vision, environment, components, lines of action, outputs, activities and indicators. It explains how these elements relate.

The Arabic-language back cover of the toolkit, noting the growing role of ICT in health services and describing the toolkit as a practical guide for governments to develop an eHealth vision, action plan and monitoring framework. The opening line is garbled OCR.
